finding.claim: /checkout computes the charge from client-supplied price and qty. An attacker can set price to a tiny value to pay almost nothing for goods. They can also use negative price or qty to get a zero or negative total, which may issue a refund or credit to the account. Nothing validates the values or looks prices up on the server.
finding.source: req.body.items[].price and req.body.items[].qty (attacker-controlled JSON body of POST /checkout)
finding.sink: req.payments.charge(req.user.id, total) at cart.js:6, which charges the attacker-computed total

trace.note: POST /checkout handler accepts the request body
total = sum(i.price * i.qty) using only client-supplied fields, with no server-side catalog lookup, no numeric or range checks and no sign check
the total is passed to the payment charge
the attacker-chosen total is echoed back as the charged amount

finding.guards_checked: Looked for server-side price lookup, input validation, a minimum-total check and a positive-quantity check, and found none in this file. The only authentication reference is req.user.id, and it is not enforced here. The safer /checkout-v2 shows the intended design (catalog price, quantity clamp), but the legacy /checkout route is still mounted. Whether the router has auth middleware or payments rejects negative amounts is not visible in the repo.

verdict.reason: cart.js:5 sums client-supplied i.price * i.qty with no catalog lookup, type, range or sign checks, and cart.js:6 passes that total to req.payments.charge for any caller with a req.user (a low-privilege customer), unlike the guarded /checkout-v2 at cart.js:13-14; unseen router auth or payments-side rejection of negative amounts would not stop the tiny-price underpayment.

finding.claim: /checkout-v2 does not validate qty. A non-numeric qty such as a string or missing value makes Math.floor(NaN) return NaN, and Math.max(1, NaN) also returns NaN, so the clamp does not apply and total becomes NaN. Infinity is also unchecked. An attacker may exploit this if the payment layer treats NaN as zero or skips the charge, but that depends on payments.charge. The same route does not check that items is an array or that sku values are valid.
finding.source: req.body.items[].qty, and also req.body.items and sku (attacker-controlled JSON body of POST /checkout-v2)
finding.sink: req.payments.charge(req.user.id, total) at cart.js:16, called with a possibly NaN or Infinity total

trace.note: iterates the client-supplied items array with no Array.isArray check
price comes from the server catalog (good), but sku is client-controlled and unvalidated
Math.max(1, Math.floor(i.qty)) returns NaN for a non-numeric qty, which poisons total; a very large qty also gives an unbounded total
charge is called with the NaN total and no isFinite or positive check
response returns charged: NaN, and JSON serializes it as null

finding.guards_checked: The Math.max(1, ...) clamp blocks negative and zero quantities, but not NaN. There is no Number.isFinite(total) or total > 0 check before charging, and no upper bound on quantity. The behavior of payments.charge and any upstream auth or validation middleware are outside the repo. This finding is lower confidence than BIZ-1 because the outcome depends on how payments.charge handles NaN.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo; Math.max(1, Math.floor(i.qty)) at cart.js:14 clamps only numeric values below 1 and does not stop NaN or Infinity. No isFinite or total > 0 check before charge at cart.js:16.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: cart.js:14 turns a missing or non-numeric qty into NaN and cart.js:16 passes it to charge without a check. The attacker only needs to be an authenticated user, since cart.js:16 uses req.user.id. Whether this gives a free or underpriced order depends on how req.payments.charge handles NaN or Infinity, and that code is outside the repo, so I can't decide it.
